questions.question: In the EOQ model with constant known demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$, no shortages and a fixed lead time $L$ between placing and receiving an order, how does the optimal order quantity compare with the classical EOQ $\sqrt{2KD/h}$ without lead time?
options: It increases by $DL$, the demand during the lead time
It becomes $\sqrt{2KD(1+L)/h}$, growing with $L$
It decreases, since stock is held for a shorter time
It is the same, $y^*=\sqrt{2KD/h}$, for every $L$

questions.question: In the EOQ model with constant known demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$, no shortages and a fixed lead time $L$ between placing and receiving an order, and $L$ shorter than the cycle length $t_0^*$, why is the order placed when on-hand stock falls to $DL$?
options: Demand uses $DL$ units during the delay, so stock hits 0 on arrival
At level $DL$ exactly $L$ cycles of stock remain before the next delivery
Level $DL$ keeps a safety stock of $DL$ units when the batch arrives
Ordering at $DL$ makes the order quantity equal to $y^*-DL$ units

questions.question: In the EOQ model with constant known demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$, no shortages and a fixed lead time $L$ between placing and receiving an order, why is the minimum relevant cost per unit time the same as without a lead time?
options: The extra stock held during the lead time is free of holding cost
Setup cost is charged per day, so the delay is cancelled out
Orders arrive at stock-outs, so the stock pattern is the same sawtooth
The extra stock on order is paid for by fewer orders per year

questions.question: In the EOQ model with constant known demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$, no shortages and a fixed lead time $L$ between placing and receiving an order, a shop opens with no stock and $L$ longer than one cycle. Why does the rule 'order $y^*$ when on-hand stock falls to $DL_e$' not cover the first weeks?
options: The rule needs no adaptation, as it already holds from day 0
The rule describes steady state, with earlier orders already in transit
The rule fails because $L_e$ is undefined when the shop opens
The rule makes the shop order $y^*$ every day until stock arrives

questions.question: Weekly demand is $D=50$ units, setup cost $K=64$ per order, holding cost $h=1$ per unit per week, and an order arrives 1 week after it is placed; no shortages are allowed. Which policy is optimal?
options: Order 130 units when stock falls to 50 units
Order 80 units when stock reaches 0 units
Order 50 units whenever stock falls to 80 units
Order 80 units when stock falls to 50 units

questions.question: An EOQ policy receives a batch every 30 days, at the moment stock runs out; each order takes $L=8$ days to arrive and demand is constant. Counting from a delivery as day 0, on which day of the cycle is the next order placed?
options: On day 8
On day 38
On day 22
On day 30

questions.question: Demand is $D=20$ units per day and each order of $y^*=100$ units starts a new cycle; an order arrives $L=12$ days after it is placed and no shortages are allowed. At which on-hand stock level is an order placed in steady state?
options: 40 units
240 units
140 units
100 units

questions.question: A shop sells 70 units per week at a constant rate and orders 140 units at a time; each order arrives 3 days after it is placed, and shortages are not allowed. At what on-hand stock level, in units, should it reorder?
options: 110 units
210 units
10 units
30 units

questions.question: In the EOQ model with constant known demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$, no shortages and a fixed lead time $L$ between placing and receiving an order, and $L$ shorter than the cycle, a cautious buyer orders $y^*$ units whenever stock falls to $DL+20$ instead of $DL$. What happens in steady state?
options: Each batch arrives too late and the shop runs out for a while
Nothing changes, since the batch size is still $y^*$
Each batch arrives with 20 units left, raising holding cost
Orders become more frequent, since the trigger is reached sooner

questions.question: In the EOQ model with constant known demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$, no shortages and a fixed lead time $L$ between placing and receiving an order, suppose $L>t_0^*=y^*/D$. Why can the order not be triggered when on-hand stock falls to $DL$?
options: $DL$ is too low, so the order arrives after the stock-out
$DL$ exceeds $y^*$, so on-hand stock never reaches it
$DL$ is allowed, but raises the cost above $\sqrt{2KDh}$
$DL$ is allowed, but needs a larger batch than $y^*$

questions.question: In the EOQ model with constant known demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$, no shortages and a fixed lead time $L$ between placing and receiving an order, the lead time $L$ is below the cycle length $t_0^*=\sqrt{2K/(Dh)}$. Demand doubles while $K$, $h$ and $L$ stay fixed and the EOQ is recomputed. How does the reorder level change?
options: It doubles to $2DL$, if $L$ is still below the new, shorter cycle
It always doubles to $2DL$, whatever the new cycle length is
It grows by the factor $\sqrt{2}$, just like the order quantity $y^*$
It stays $DL$, since the lead time $L$ itself has not changed

questions.question: An EOQ policy has a cycle of $t_0^*=8$ days, each batch arriving as stock runs out, and a lead time of $L=19$ days under constant demand. How many days after each delivery is the next order placed?
options: 11 days
3 days
5 days
0 days

questions.question: In the EOQ model with constant known demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$, no shortages and a fixed lead time $L$ between placing and receiving an order, the optimal batch is still $y^*=\sqrt{2KD/h}$. Which assumption is essential for the lead time to leave the batch size unchanged?
options: Holding cost is charged on the goods in transit as well
The cost $KD/y+hy/2$ is strictly convex in $y$
The lead time is longer than one ordering cycle
Both $D$ and $L$ are known and constant over time

questions.question: In the EOQ model with constant known demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$, no shortages and a fixed lead time $L$ between placing and receiving an order, the lead time is exactly two cycles, $L=2t_0^*$. At which on-hand stock level is an order placed?
options: At $DL_e=0$, the very moment a batch arrives
At $2y^*$, the demand during the lead time
At $Dt_0^*=y^*$, the stock just after a delivery
At no level, since $L_e$ is not defined here

questions.question: A shop sells 30 units per day, orders 300 units at a time and reorders at 120 units, planned for a lead time of 4 days. One delivery arrives after 5 days instead. How many units of demand cannot be met from stock in that cycle?
options: 0 units
120 units
30 units
150 units

questions.question: With setup cost 50 and holding cost 1 per unit per week, an EOQ policy uses cycle $t_0^*=\sqrt{2K/(Dh)}$ and lead time 1.5 weeks. Demand rises from 25 to 100 units per week and the EOQ is recomputed. At which on-hand stock level is an order now placed?
options: 150 units
50 units
100 units
37.5 units
